claims.text: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially exists in a high-temperature BCC phase.
The stability of BCC versus secondary phases in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 is governed by competition between a composition-dependent free-energy driving force and kinetic barriers to atomic rearrangement.
The free-energy difference between BCC and alternative phases has a maximum at an intermediate temperature.
An isothermal hold at that intermediate temperature allows diffusion to overcome kinetic barriers and drive transformation from BCC.
Atomic diffusion and local atomic rearrangements mediate the transition from metastable BCC to secondary phases.
Sufficient isothermal holding and moderate cooling allow the thermodynamic driving force to overcome kinetic constraints.
Slower cooling or holding near the critical transformation temperature permits phase transformation to progress.
Rapid cooling kinetically locks in the high-temperature BCC structure of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7.
Controlled cooling with an appropriate hold will produce the onset and gradual growth of secondary phases or a two-phase mixture.
The transformation will generate detectable diffraction and calorimetric signals.
Rapid quenching will retain nearly 100% of the high-temperature BCC phase.
The proposed behavior applies where the BCC-to-alternative-phase free-energy difference is significant and atomic diffusion remains active.
At extremely low temperatures, diffusion is effectively frozen.
Sufficient Al additions to Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys can produce phase transformations and partially ordered aluminides in a BCC matrix.
Differences in Gibbs free energy between BCC and FCC phases can predict composition- and temperature-dependent phase fractions and transformation rates in a multicomponent alloy.
Cooling rate can strongly affect phase selection in high-entropy alloys.
Extremely rapid solidification can suppress secondary phases that appear at slower cooling rates.
